 How merchants can reduce holiday card-not-present fraud without losing legitimate customers 
 Payments 
 How merchants can reduce holiday card-not-present fraud without losing legitimate customers
 October 29, 2026
 Holiday shopping volume gives fraud more places to hide. Targeted controls can help address card-not-present fraud and card testing, while limiting unnecessary declines and protecting revenue and the customer experience.
 Overview
 8 min read
 Key takeaways 
 Holiday volume can make card-not-present fraud, card testing and automated attacks harder to distinguish from typical transaction activity. Stronger controls work best when they stay targeted. 
 Risk-based monitoring and layered checks can help protect against fraud without creating unnecessary false declines or hurting approval rates.
 Looking across fraud losses, approvals, chargebacks and review workload can give merchants a clearer view of how well their controls are performing.
 $257.8 B 
 U.S. online holiday spending from November 1 through December 31, 2025, was up 6.8% year over year, according to Adobe Analytics. 1 
 For e-commerce merchants, one of the biggest concerns is card-not-present (CNP) fraud, which involves using payment credentials fraudulently when the physical card isn’t presented.
 Fraud pressure tends to rise when merchants are busiest. CNP fraud, card testing, chargeback abuse and automated attacks can all increase operational strain at the same time teams are trying to keep checkout moving.
 144% 
 More suspected fraudulent activity was blocked by certain card networks globally over the 2025 Black Friday and Cyber Monday weekend than during the same period a year earlier. 2 
 Merchants balance CNP fraud prevention with the customer experience. Controls ideally reduce losses while preserving legitimate approvals, authorization rates and revenue.
 Why does card-not-present fraud increase during holiday shopping? 
 Peak shopping periods give fraudsters more activity to blend into. A sudden increase in transactions can make unusual behavior harder to isolate, while operations teams have less time to investigate each exception. 
 Card testing is an automated fraud tactic in which stolen or compromised card credentials are tested through low-dollar transactions to determine whether they’re active. Attackers may then use validated credentials for fraudulent purchases. 3   CNP fraud can be difficult to distinguish from valid e-commerce activity because the transaction itself may look ordinary. 
 High holiday volumes can also make automated attacks harder to isolate. That makes transaction context increasingly important. Customer, payment and transaction patterns can help merchants identify activity that may warrant additional review.
 What does holiday card-not-present fraud look like? 
 Fraud during peak shopping periods can take several forms. Merchants may see compromised cards used for online purchases, bursts of low-value card-testing attempts or dispute abuse that surfaces after an order has been fulfilled.
 AI can make fraudulent activity easier to automate and scale. During peak shopping periods, higher volumes can make that activity harder to distinguish from normal customer behavior. 4 That puts more pressure on merchants to identify risk without adding unnecessary friction for legitimate customers. 
 The financial impact can extend well beyond the original purchase. The FBI reports that credit card fraud accounted for $282 million in losses in 2025, while non-payment and non-delivery scams resulted in more than $503 million in losses. 5 The agency also notes that complaint volume often rises in the early months of the year, suggesting a connection to holiday-season scams. 
 Fraud tactics are evolving fast
 Learn more
 How can merchants reduce fraud without increasing false declines? 
 Tightening controls across the board may help protect against some fraud, but it can also create unnecessary friction for customers. 
 Overly restrictive controls can create false declines — where legitimate transactions are rejected as suspicious—and reduce authorization rates, the share of transactions approved. 6 During the holidays, that added friction comes at a particularly important point in the customer journey. 
 A more targeted approach applies additional scrutiny where risk is higher, while allowing lower-risk activity to move with less interruption. Using multiple checks can support that balance by bringing together different signals rather than relying on a single rule or threshold. 7 
 Merchants can also adjust controls as behavior changes throughout the season. A pattern that looks unusual in October may be completely normal during a major shopping weekend. That balance can help merchants respond to changing fraud patterns without adding unnecessary friction at checkout. 
 How fraud can affect revenue, operations and customer trust 
 Chargebacks can create work long after the original purchase. Teams may need to investigate disputes, gather documentation and respond within network timelines, adding costs that can affect the bottom line. Card-testing attacks can create additional processing costs and may also lead to payment network monitoring, chargebacks and potential fines. 8 
 False declines create a different kind of loss. A shopper whose purchase is incorrectly declined may abandon it entirely, reducing revenue and potentially weakening the customer relationship. 
 There’s also a broader confidence issue. Customers expect payment experiences to feel both secure and easy. Fraud controls that add checkout steps or delays can work against that experience, while streamlined payments can support customer loyalty. 9 
 That’s why fraud performance should be considered alongside authorization rates, dispute levels and customer experience. Looking across fraud losses, false declines, chargebacks, conversion and review workload can give merchants a fuller picture of how their controls are performing.
 How can merchants prepare for peak-season fraud? 
 Preparation starts before transaction volumes rise. Merchants can focus on a few areas as peak season approaches:
 Historical fraud and dispute patterns can show where exceptions tend to cluster.
 Monitoring changes in transaction activity, declines and card testing can help teams spot seasonal shifts. 10 
 Controls can be adjusted as seasonal patterns change, so expected increases in volume do not automatically trigger unnecessary declines.
 Clear escalation processes can help teams understand how suspicious activity should be handled.
 Technology plays an important role, but the surrounding processes matter just as much. Fraud tools should support secure, compliant payment experiences while giving teams enough visibility to understand why activity is being flagged and how controls are performing.
 Frequently asked questions 
 What is card-not-present fraud? 
 Card-not-present fraud occurs when stolen or compromised payment credentials are used without the physical card being presented, commonly in e-commerce or other remote transactions.
 What is card testing? 
 Card testing uses small, repeated authorization attempts to determine whether stolen card credentials are still active. Successful credentials may then be used for larger fraudulent purchases.
 How can merchants reduce fraud without increasing false declines? 
 Risk-based controls can apply more scrutiny to higher-risk activity while allowing lower-risk transactions to move with less friction. Monitoring performance across fraud losses, false declines and authorization rates can help merchants understand whether controls are working as intended.
 Which metrics should merchants monitor during peak shopping? 
 Useful measures include fraud loss, false-decline rates, authorization or approval rates, chargeback rates, conversion and manual-review workload. Looking at those measures together gives a more complete picture than relying on one metric alone.
 The bottom line 
 Holiday shopping creates a narrow window in which merchants need to move quickly without losing control of risk. The strongest fraud strategies are built around that balance: identifying high-risk activity early while keeping valid customers moving.
 That requires monitoring, adaptable controls and a clear view of how fraud decisions affect approvals, disputes and customer experience. 
 Fraud tactics will continue to evolve. Preparing early and adapting controls as patterns change can help merchants respond without adding unnecessary checkout friction or losing sight of customer trust and growth.
